section_1.title: What is a Vector? (The 'Arrow' Intuition)
section_1.content: Introduce vectors as directed line segments representing both magnitude (length) and direction. Contrast this with scalars (simple numbers). Use a visual coordinate system where an arrow starts at the origin (0,0).
section_1.example: A drone pilot moving 5 meters North-East. The arrow represents the flight path; the length is the speed/distance, and the orientation is the heading.

section_2.title: Vector Representation and Components
section_2.content: Explain breaking a vector into its horizontal (x) and vertical (y) components. Visualize this by drawing a right-angled triangle where the vector is the hypotenuse. Emphasize that any vector [a, b] is just a sequence of moves on a grid.
section_2.example: Representing a jumping cat as a vector [3, 4], where it moves 3 units across the room and 4 units vertically onto a shelf.

section_3.title: Vector Addition: The Tip-to-Tail Method
section_3.content: Explain how to combine two vectors. Visually slide the second vector so its tail sits on the tip of the first. The resulting 'shortcut' arrow is the sum. This builds the intuition for spatial navigation.
section_3.example: A robot dog walking 2 steps forward, then 3 steps right. The final position relative to the start is the 'resultant' vector.

section_4.title: Scaling: Changing Magnitude
section_4.content: Define scalar multiplication. Multiplying by a constant 'k' stretches or shrinks the vector. A negative 'k' reverses the direction. Show this animation as the arrow growing or flipping 180 degrees.
section_4.example: A game character receiving a 'speed boost' power-up, represented by multiplying their movement vector [1, 1] by 2, resulting in [2, 2].

section_5.title: Summary and Real-World Application
section_5.content: Briefly recap: Vectors store position/force, can be decomposed, added, and scaled. Connect this to modern technology like game physics engines and GPS navigation.
section_5.example: In a video game, the character's velocity vector is continuously updated by adding 'gravity' vectors and 'jump' vectors to calculate the frame-by-frame position.
